All Major UK Parties Now Have Supporters Of Legalizing Marijuana;
The Government Remains Loyal To DEAland.
Tory Leader "Infuriated." When He Is Angry, He Is Almost Visible.

(Marijuananews note: The real significance of this story is that there are prominent members of three major parties in the UK Parliament who have come out in favor of either legalizing marijuana or a Royal Commission. The Blair government’s first loyalty is to DEAland prohibitionism, but this is no longer a "fringe issue" even though this article twice describes it as "radical."

The prohibitionist bias of the reporting here would make this piece more appropriate for an editorial page.)

September 22, 1999
From The Daily Mail
letters@dailymail.co.uk
http://www.dailymail.co.uk/

HAGUE INFURIATED OVER LILLEY'S CALL ON CANNABIS

WILLIAM HAGUE slapped down Peter Lilley last night after the former deputy Tory leader indicated he will call for the decriminalisation of cannabis.
(Marijuananews note: The Tories are the Conservatives, Margaret Thatcher’s party, also the Party of Churchill and Burke. Hague is supposedly their leader. He would be Prime Minister if the Tories were to win the next election. He has about as much chance of being the next king.)

Mr Lilley, who was dropped from the shadow cabinet over the summer, has been moving towards a radical stance on drug issues.

Now outside the constraints of shadow cabinet responsibilities, he is free to present the views that deviate so sharply from traditional Tory thinking. (Marijuananews note: Now, that is an improbable concept.)

But when news of Mr Lilley's intentions leaked last night, Mr Hague was infuriated at what he sees as another example of his former deputy's bizarre lack of political nous.
(Marijuananews note: I have no idea what nous means, either. They speak a very strange version of English in England. However, it is probably a part of "traditional Tory thinking.")

The controversy comes at a difficult time for Mr Hague desperately trying to re-establish the Tory Party as a force in main-stream politics. The spectacle of the man who only a few months ago as in charge of Tory policy proposing the decriminalisation of cannabis caused consternation at Tory headquarters yesterday.

(Marijuananews note: Opposing an obviously disastrous policy might seem like political leadership, but they really are not leaders.

As in DEAland the UK "Conservatives" get most of their ideas from libertarians. However, they avoid ideas that frighten them. Then they have to feel their way along without any coherent explanation for why they suddenly think that big government is no longer dangerous but benign even as it kills people in the war on even the sick and dying.

Of course, Blair has moved the Labor Party so far to the right that the Liberal Democratic leader recently had to warn his party not to try to go to the "left of Labor." A few years ago that would have been a joke. Nonetheless, he has called for a Royal Commission on drugs policy with the specific question about legalizing marijuana.)

Only a week ago Mr Hague told political journalists that drug dealers who are twice convicted of supplying hard drugs to children should get life sentences.
(Marijuananews note: While that is absurd posturing, such a position is by no means inconsistent with legalizing cannabis.)

Last night a spokesman for Mr Hague tried to distance the Tory leader from the embarrassment.

He said: "William's position is perfectly clear. He is firmly opposed to all forms of illegal drug taking. We are opposed to the legalisation of cannabis.

"It is crystal clear. Only a week ago Mr Hague called for tougher penalties for people pushing drugs to children. Peter Lilley is not front bencher. When he was, he fully supported the party line. What he is saying now is not the leadership's view."

Mr Lilley's decision to discuss his views in a series of speeches is seen as the act of a man still bitter at his treatment by the leadership, although he has insisted that he is still "100 per cent loyalist."

The former Tory Social Security Secretary has discussed this radical approach towards drugs policy with friends.

They looked at ways of distinguishing between people who bought cannabis for their own use and those who make a living out of hard drugs.

The Tory leadership is highly sensitive about the decriminalisation of drugs. One of Mr Hague's front bench spokesmen, Alan Duncan, dropped a chapter on his own views on drugs from a book last year.
